stages.name: Protectionism and efficiency
stages.title: Protectionism and efficiency
stages.sub: Why shielding domestic firms from foreign competition can dull their drive to improve.

steps.q: A tariff on imported steel means foreign steel is now much more expensive here. Do domestic steel firms still need to worry about losing customers to cheaper foreign steel?
steps.right: No, they are protected from that competition
steps.wrong: Yes, foreign steel is still just as much of a threat
steps.hint: The tariff already raises the foreign firms' prices for them. Who still has an edge?
steps.pre: So the domestic firms are now

steps.q: If foreign rivals can no longer easily undercut them on price, what pushes the domestic firms to cut costs or improve their product?
steps.right: Very little, the usual pressure has gone
steps.wrong: The same strong pressure as before
steps.hint: Think about what normally forces firms to innovate: rivals taking their customers. Is that rival threat still there?

steps.q: With customers guaranteed and little threat of losing them, how hard is a protected firm's management likely to work at spotting new efficiencies?
steps.right: Not very hard, they can get comfortable
steps.wrong: Just as hard as before, guaranteed customers change nothing
steps.hint: If nothing forces you to try harder, what tends to happen to effort over time?

steps.q: Compare this protected, comfortable firm to one facing full foreign competition (which pushes firms to keep innovating). Over time, which firm is more likely to fall behind on efficiency and new ideas?
steps.right: The protected firm, its incentive to innovate is weaker
steps.wrong: The firm facing full competition, since it has more rivals to worry about
steps.hint: Remember competition drives innovation. Take that driver away and what happens to the incentive to improve?
